newsitem.title: USA: Freshmen Republicans suffer small losses.
newsitem.headline: Freshmen Republicans suffer small losses.

text.p: Most of the Republican freshmen who swept their party into control of the House of Representatives two years ago survived Tuesday's voting despite a massive effort by Democrats and organised labour to unseat them.
With a handful of House races still undecided on Wednesday, projected returns point to losses by no more than 15 of the 70 freshmen Republicans seeking re-election.

The freshmen were key to House Speaker Newt Gingrich's revolution and voted to keep the government shut down last January when even Gingrich had decided to compromise with President Bill Clinton on budget issues.
Labour unions targeted many of the freshmen in this year's election campaigns, spending millions of dollars on advertising to boost Democratic challengers.

"We won the big prize, continued control of the House," Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Bill Paxon said in conceding at least 13 losses by House freshmen, including three in Washington state and two in North Carolina.
Another freshman, Jon Fox of Pennsylvania, leads his race by only 10 votes with a recount set for Friday while Texas freshman Steve Stockman faces a runoff in December.
In Michigan, Democrat Debbie Stabenow, one of those who got heavy labour support, defeated Republican Dick Chrysler and Democrat Walter Capps ousted Republican Andrea Seastrand in California.

In Washington, where six Republican freshmen won in 1994, Randy Tate was defeated by Democrat Adam Smith and Linda Smith and Jack Metcalf were trailing in their races. But first-termers Rick White, Doc Hastings and George Nethercutt all won. Oregon freshman Jim Bunn was also trailing.

Republicans lost the Chicago seat held by Representative Michael Flanagan to Democrat Rod Blagojevich. Flanagan was dismissed as the "accidental congressman" who brought down veteran Democratic Representative Dan Rostenkowski who was convicted for misuse of congressional funds. The district is heavily Democratic.

A strong stand for gun control gave New York Democrat Carolyn McCarthy a win over Republican Representative Dan Frisa. McCarthy's husband was killed in an attack by a gunman on a subway and her son suffered brain damage. She entered the race after Frisa refused to endorse gun control measures.
In Ohio, Frank Cremeans, lost to Democrat Ted Strickland, 51 percent to 49 percent.

North Carolina freshman David Funderburk was one of the Democratic party's main targets and lost to Democrat Bobby Etheridge, a state official. Funderburk faced charges that he had been the driver during an auto accident but switched seats to avoid blame. He had been politically allied with Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, who won a fifth term.
Fred Heineman who represented the Raleigh-Chapel Hill area lost in a rematch with former Democratic Representative David Price who charged that Republican votes with Gingrich hurt the district.
New Jersey Representative Bill Martini, who won by the narrowest of margins in 1994, was turned out by Democrat William Pascrell whose campaign linked the Republican to Gingrich.

Representative James Longley of Maine, closely allied with Gingrich, lost to Democrat Tom Allen, a former mayor of Portland who said the Republican's views were too conservative for the district which had tended to elect moderates.
Republican National Committee chairman Haley Barbour said voters sent Washington a mixed message with the re-election of Clinton while Republicans held control of Congress.
But White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta told television networks the message was a call for bipartisan compromise on legislation.
"The American people, frankly, are sick of gridlock and partisanship and the kind of political attacks and personal attacks that we've seen," he said.

Three of the 73 freshmen Republicans did not seek re-election to the House. Sam Brownback was elected to the Senate from Kansas and Enid Greene of Utah and Wes Cooley of Oregon did not run due to scandals involving their 1994 campaigns, but Republicans held on to all three seats.
